newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Expansion to test ASEAN unity -Australian study.
newsitem.headline: Expansion to test ASEAN unity -Australian study.

text.p: ASEAN's expansion to include all southeast Asian countries could test the regional club's unity and relations with the West, but would offer lucrative economic gains, an Australian government study said on Friday.
The Association of South East Asian Nations' (ASEAN) decision to admit Burma posed particular problems, the East Asia Analytical Unit report warned.
Burma, Laos and Cambodia will join the grouping in July, expanding the bloc to include all 10 southeast Asian countries.
Vietnam became the seventh member in 1995, joining Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand.
"New members may test ASEAN's consensus decision-making," said the unit's report on the integration of the three newest members and Vietnam.

"Burma's membership may strain cohesion, solidarity and ASEAN's relations with the rest of the world, particularly the United States and European Union, both of which have instituted sanctions against Burma's military regime."

Burma's military rule, human rights abuses and suppression of democracy movements have drawn world-wide criticism, but ASEAN has followed a policy of "constructive engagement" that seeks to improve the situation through cooperative dealings.
Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer on Thursday urged ASEAN members to press Rangoon to improve human rights.

"I will continue to encourage them to give real effect to their constructive engagement policy by using their new relationship with Burmese leaders to express the very real concerns that I know they have about the human rights situation in Burma," he said in a speech.
The report said the new members, including Vietnam, would provide an economic boost for all 10 ASEAN members.
"The new members increase trade complementarity within ASEAN and enhance the regional division of labour based on comparative advantage," the study said.
"This increases opportunities for trade and investment."
The report said a larger ASEAN would stimulate further economic reforms in member countries and give the group more economic weight and greater access to world markets.
A 10-member ASEAN creates a bloc with a population of 500 million people with combined gross domestic product of US$650 million.
